title: Why You Wouldn't Survive a Night in a Victorian Doss-House in 1888
fullText: London 1888. The cheapest bed in the richest city on earth is a wooden box shaped like a coffin. It costs four pants [music] a night and men queue in the rain for it. Daniel is 23. He unloaded ships for 10 hours today and it paid him five pennies. They're in his fist right now. his bed, his breakfast, his entire tomorrow held in one closed hand outside a lodging house door in White Chapel. [music] Inside there is a menu. A bench costs one penny, but sleeping on it is forbidden. A rope costs two. The coffin costs four. Outside is free. Outside is the one that [music] kills. Tonight you'll learn the rules of London's strangest institution. rebuilt from the diary of a journalist who went undercover in these rooms and the police registers of the men who never left them. By dawn, you'll understand why the poorest men in the empire [music] paid to sleep in a coffin and why the most dangerous thing in this house was falling asleep. The door opens before Daniel knocks. The man filling the frame is called the deputy. Every doss house in London has one. He is not the owner. The owner lives somewhere the smell can't reach and collects his money once a night through a locked box. The deputy is the owner's fist. Doorman, rent collector, judge, and [music] jury, usually with a poker within reach, and the memory of every face that has ever cheated him. In some houses, the deputy is a woman, and the lodgers learn fast that this changes nothing at all. Above his head, a painted canvas sign, a real one from Flower and Dean Street, [music] read like this. The original little wonder lodgings for single men, four pence. Good double beds, 8 pint per night. Good is doing work in that sentence [music] that no word should be asked to do. Daniel opens his fist. Four of his five pennies cross the doorstep. Understand the first law of this house. There is no credit here. Not a farthing. Not for one night. Not if the deputy has known you 10 years. Not if it's snowing. The rule is older than the paint on the sign. Money first or the door shuts. The deputy has heard every story in London and he has stopped hearing them. And this door is not rare. This is a system. In White Chapel alone, one district. There are 233 of these houses [music] registered with the police. And tonight they will hold over 8,000 sleepers. An industry of fourpences. A city within the city run from doorsteps by men like this one. The deputy drops Daniel's pennies through the slot of a wooden box. Then he jerks his thumb down the corridor [music] toward the one room every dosser goes first. Not the beds. The beds can wait. The room with the fire where the men who still have their forpants sit beside the men who don't. And by midnight, one of those men will follow Daniel upstairs. The corridor ends in heat. The kitchen is the heart of every doss house. And it is below the street, a cellar reached by a ladder stair lit by one thing only, a coke fire that has not gone out in years. The deputy keeps it burning the way a church keeps a flame. It is the single free luxury this institution offers. And everything in the room bends toward it. 20 men and women are down here. A Nav'i frying three herrings on a borrowed pan. An old flower seller drying her boots on the fender. Steam rising off the leather. A boy of maybe nine, asleep [music] sitting up, who was born into houses like this, and has never slept anywhere else. Whole childhoods happen in this cellar. Daniel buys nothing. He has one penny left and a decision to make with it. supper tonight or bread tomorrow. He sits on a bench near the fire and he keeps [music] that penny inside his closed fist inside his coat pocket. And he is right to because look at the men by the wall. Three of them not sitting, pacing, hands in empty pockets, eyes going to the door every time it opens. The deputy lets regulars sit by his fire for nothing. But at midnight sitting [music] ends. These men are a half penny short or a whole fourpint short and they are waiting for a friend to walk in. Someone, anyone who might lend the coppers that complete their doss money. A 19-year-old journalist who slept in these rooms undercover wrote down what happens next. Most nights the friend never comes. And one by one, the pacing men stop pacing, pull their collars up, [music] and shuffle out to spend the night under the sky. Daniel watches the third man go, and he doesn't know it yet. But before this night ends, the difference between that man's night and his own will come down to something smaller than forpants. Midnight. The deputy bangs a poker on the stair rail and the room sorts itself by money because this house has a menu and it is the strangest menu in the British Empire. One penny buys the bench Daniel is sitting on for the whole night, but a penny buys sitting only. Sleep is not included. In the penny situp, the rule is enforced exactly as it sounds. You may rest, you may lean, but the moment your eyes close and your body slides, you are woken [music] all night. For some men, that torture is still better than the street because the street has rain. Two pennies buys the rope. Charles Dickens described it 50 years before this night, and his description survives. strips of coarse sacking [music] stretched between two ropes running the length of a room. A row of men lying on cloth hammocks inches [music] apart and the wakeup call is built into the furniture. At 6 every morning, the ropes are let go at one end. The whole row of sleeping men drops. The house empties itself. Four pennies, Daniel's price, buys a box on the floor. We'll meet it in a moment. Eight pennies buys a good double bed. And here the menu turns darkest of all. In the worst houses, a bed is not a thing you rent. It's a thing you share. In shifts, three strangers, one mattress, 8 hours each, a relay of bodies that never lets the sheets go cold. Some beds in this city have not been empty in years. [music] Daniel climbs the stairs with the four pony men. At the top, the deputy pulls open a door and Daniel looks into the room he has paid for and stops walking because nobody forgets the first time they see it. 40 coffins laid out in rows and most of them already full. 40 wooden boxes in four rows filling a long room wall to wall. Each one is 6 ft by two. The dimensions are exactly what your [music] eyes think they are. Nobody who runs these houses apologizes for it. The shape is simply the most efficient way [music] to pack sleeping humans onto a floor. And efficiency is the only architecture the poor are offered. Daniel finds an empty box in the second row and lowers himself in. The wood is hard but flat and [music] flat is the entire luxury he has purchased. The penny men are upright on their bench. [music] The rope men are folded over sacking. Daniel gets to lie on his back at full length. And after 10 hours of hauling cargo, that geometry is worth every farthing of the four he paid. With the box comes a blanket, not wool, leather, or oiled tarpolin, stiff as a sail. There's a reason, and the reason is the box's one great floor. Men who slept in these rooms all wrote down the same complaint almost word for word. The bugs. Every doss house in London has them. But a man in an open bed can at least turn away. A man in a box is enclosed with them. Wool blankets carry the colony from sleeper to sleeper. Leather can be wiped clean with a bucket by morning. The blanket isn't for comfort. It's quarantine. [music] Around him, the room fills. The herring navi two boxes down already snoring. The flower cellar against the far wall, boots still on. The 9-year-old from the kitchen, curled in a box near the door. In the only bedroom his whole life has ever had, the candle at the stair goes out. [music] And in the darkness, Daniel does what every man in this room did before closing his eyes. The one ritual that decides whether he'll still own anything at dawn. The ritual is this. Boots off, but never on the floor. On the floor, they're gone by morning. Boots go under your head, heels down, and they are your pillow now. Coat off, folded, laid over your chest under the leather blanket, a second layer, and harder to slide off a sleeping man than one hanging on a nail. And the last penny, Daniel's supper or breakfast penny, stays where it has been all [music] night inside his fist inside his pocket. A man can steal almost anything from a sleeper except the inside of his closed hand. Every man in this room performed some version of the same ceremony because everyone knows what Forpants also buys. [music] Entry. The thief pays the same coin Daniel paid, receives the same box, and waits for the same darkness. For him, the doss house isn't shelter. It's a hunting ground with 40 unconscious targets prepaid. And if something is taken, nothing happens. The police register these houses, inspect these houses, and stand outside these houses. A dosser reporting a stolen coat learns quickly what the law thinks a dosser's coat is worth. In here, property law is a pair of heels under your own skull. Then nothing happens for a while. Truly nothing. 2 in the morning. The room breathes. 40 chests rising out of rhythm. A cough traveling down the rose like weather. The coke fires glow climbing the ladder stair. and laying one soft orange line under the door. Somewhere below the deputy's chair caks. Daniel lies in his box, boots under his skull, fist closed, [music] listening to a whole hidden city sleeping around him. And for one hour, the most dangerous house in White Chapel is almost peaceful. Almost. Because a few streets away in a lodging house kitchen just like the one downstairs, a woman is being told to leave over forpants she doesn't have. Hold that woman in your mind. We're coming to her. But first, you need to understand the strangest fact about the room Daniel is sleeping in. Everything in it is legal. The box, the bugs, the relay beds, the penny bench where sleep is forbidden. All of it registered, licensed, [music] and inspected by the Metropolitan Police under an act of Parliament passed in 1851 precisely to make houses like this one [music] decent. The law requires the keeper to lime wash the walls twice a [music] year, to report fever to the authorities, to hang the maximum number of sleepers per room on a card, and to let a police inspector walk through at any hour he pleases. And the inspectors come. They count the boxes. They check the card. [music] They note the lime wash. Then they sign the register of a house where 40 humans sleep in coffins. [music] And they leave because the card is accurate and the walls are white. It is squalor [music] with paperwork. Misery up to code. Queen Victoria herself wanted [music] these houses abolished. Dens of thieves, the respectable said. And here is the twist [music] the respectable never understood. The dossers defended them because the empire's official alternative was the workhouse. Free shelter at the price of your liberty. The workhouse split husbands from [music] wives, put porpas in uniform, and locked the door behind them. The doss house asked one question only. Have you got forpants? And in the whole of Victorian England, [music] there was no other door that asked so little, no sermon, no shame, no name taken, [music] just forpants. Which is exactly why in this one year, 1888, forpants became the most important sum of money in the world. Because a few streets from Daniel's box, a woman doesn't have it. Her name is Mary Anne Nicholls. The lodging houses know her as Polly. She is 43 [music] and tonight she is sitting in the warm kitchen of Wilmott, a doss house at 18th Street, 10 minutes walk from Daniel's box and the only lodging house in White Chapel that takes women only. [music] For a woman alone in this district, that makes it the safest room in the East End. She is beside the fire. She is almost home. Then the deputy asks the question every deputy asks and her pockets answer it. Fourpants short. The rule is older than the paint. [music] No credit. Not for a regular. Not at 1:00 in the morning. Not for her. She is shown out of the warmth. Past the fire. [music] Through the door. What happens to the ones the rule turns out? London has an unofficial map for them. The parks until the police sweep through the embankment benches, the doorways where sleeping is itself an offense a constable can move you on for. In the coldest months, some walk in circles until sunrise, because walking is legal, and lying down is not. That is the floor beneath the dos house floor. Below the penny bench, there is only motion. Polly isn't worried. [music] She has earned her DOSs money before, and she will earn it again tonight. And she has a [music] new black bonnet that makes her feel lucky. Her last recorded words at that door are almost cheerful. Never mind. I'll soon get my Doss money. See what a jolly bonnet I've got now. She walks out into the small hours of August the 31st, 1888. A strange storm broken night. The sky over the docks glowing red from two great fires burning on the river. She never comes back. Before sunrise, she is found in a gateway on Bucks Row, the first name of the most infamous autumn London has ever known. And when the world's newspapers descend on White Chapel demanding how, the trail leads them again and again to the same unglamorous answer, a four pony bed, and the people who couldn't reach it. The change begins the same year with the strangest reform in the history of charity. In 1888, the Salvation Army opens [music] its first food and shelter depot in the docklands on the West India Dock Road. And when [music] respectable England finally walks inside to see the rescue, it finds a penny bench, a row of coffin-shaped boxes [music] with leather blankets, the very furniture of the Doss House. Because here is the truth that separates the reformers [music] who talked from the ones who slept among the poor. The penny situp and the four penny [music] coffin were not the problem. They were the improvement. The army's coffins were clean. The blankets were scrubbed. The room was warmed by steam pipes. The floors washed. The bugs actually fought. And the forpants bought something no little wonder ever included. Hot coffee and bread at 7 at night and again at 7 in the morning before the day's search for work began. [music] Same box, same price, different world. From there the ladder gets built one rung at a time. [music] Within four years, the first roten house opens. A working man's hotel at 6 pence a night for an actual cubicle, a locker, a washroom, and men queue around the block for [music] it. The county council starts building. The doss house, squeezed between better options, spends the next [music] half century slowly dying, and one piece of it never died at all. Walk through East London tonight and you can still hear it. Doss, dosser, dossing [music] down, a for pony word minted in these rooms, still circulating a century and a half later. But Daniel knows nothing of what's coming. All he knows is the sound every dosser dreads, boots on the stairs before the sun is fully up. 6:00. The deputy's boots come up the stairs and his poker beats [music] the rail like a bell. Turn out. No exceptions, no extensions. The forpants expired at dawn. In the rope rooms across White Chapel, [music] this is the moment the ropes are let go and whole rows of men drop into the morning. Daniel sits up in his box. Boots still under his skull. Coat still on his chest and in his fist uncurling finger by finger one [music] penny. He made it through with everything he owns. And now you can see what this institution truly was. Not a bed, a loop. He'll spend that penny on bread, stand [music] at the dock gates by 7, and haul cargo for 10 hours to earn tonight's forpants, so he can hand it to the same deputy at the same door tonight. The doss house didn't shelter the poor [music] of London. It meeted them one night at a time. Remember the pacing man in the kitchen, the one who shuffled out? [music] He was a half penny short. That was the whole difference between his knight under the sky [music] and Daniel's night in the box. Not character, not effort, a half penny, smaller than four pence, exactly [music] as promised. Poly nickels was four pint short. On the one night in history it mattered most. [music] Tonight you'll walk to a door that opens because you own the key and lie down in a bed no one can turn you out of. [music] That key is the whole distance between you and Daniel. And it [music] was paid for by a century of people who decided forpants was too much to ask. If this [music] changed what a bed means to you, share it with someone who has never once thought about it and [music] tell me below. The penny bench, the two penny rope, or the four penny coffin. Which would you [music] have paid for? Subscribe to Worlds Before Us. The next room we sleep in might be the one that finally breaks you.
